## [Meet SAM (Sovereign Agent Mesh): A Zero-Config, Zero-Trust P2P Network for AI Agents](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/08/18/meet-sam-sovereign-agent-mesh-a-zero-config-zero-trust-p2p-network-for-ai-agents/)
*MarkTechPost* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: api_update, mcp, open_source

> Google has open-sourced SAM (Sovereign Agent Mesh) under Apache-2.0 — and it has nothing to do with Segment Anything. SAM is a zero-config, zero-trust P2P overlay that lets autonomous agents discover and call each other's MCP tools across cloud, on-prem, laptop and edge environments, without exposing a single internal endpoint to the public internet. Identity flows from OIDC into Biscuit capability tokens, so nodes authorize every request offline under a strict default-deny model. The post Meet SAM (Sovereign Agent Mesh): A Zero-Config, Zero-Trust P2P Network for AI Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost .

## [pnpm 12 RC 7](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v12.0.0-rc.7)
*GitHub Releases · pnpm* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: api_update, developer_tool, cli_tool

> <h2>Minor Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p><code>node_modules/.modules.yaml</code> no longer records the registries an install resolved from, and the recorded copy is dropped from the file on the first install that rewrites it.</p> <p>It dated from the lockfile format that spelled a dependency's path relative to its registry, where reading an installed tree meant knowing the registries it was installed with. Dependency paths have not carried a registry for several major versions, and the recorded copy outlived its use: <code>pnpm list</code>, <code>pnpm why</code>, and single-project installs preferred it over the project's own configuration, so a project whose registry had changed since its last install was still read through the old one.</p> <p>They now use the configured registries, like every other command already did.</p> </li> <li> <p>When <code>enableGlobalVirtualStore</code> is on, every process pnpm spawns for the project (<code>pnpm run</code>, <code>pnpm exec</code>, lifecycle scripts) now receives a <code>NODE_PATH</code> pointing at the project's hoisted <code>node_modules</code>, plus a <code>NODE_OPTIONS</code> <code>--import</code> flag that registers a resolve hook restoring <code>NODE_PATH</code> lookups for ESM imports. Dependencies that import undeclared ("phantom") packages keep resolving under the global virtual store — for both CommonJS and ESM — without installing the <code>@pnpm/plugin-esm-node-path</code> config dependency <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/9618" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/9618/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#9618</a>. Tools run by <code>pnpm dlx</code> resolve such dependencies too: the JS CLI passes them the same environment, while the Rust CLI's dlx cache is self-contained, so its layout already exposes them.</p> </li> <li> <p>A registry can now declare that its abbreviated metadata carries the <code>time</code> field, so <code>resolutionMode: time-based</code> reads the full metadata document only from the registries that need it:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-yaml notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="resolutionMode: time-based registries: https://npm.internal.example/: supportsTimeField: true"><pre><span class="pl-ent">resolutionMode</span>: <span class="pl-s">time-based</span> <span class="pl-ent">registries</span>: <span class="pl-ent">https://npm.internal.example/</span>: <span class="pl-ent">supportsTimeField</span>: <span class="pl-c1">true</span></pre></div> <p><code>registry.npmjs.org</code> omits <code>time</code> from abbreviated metadata, so a time-based resolution has to fall back to the much larger full document. That fallback used to be all-or-nothing: <code>registrySupportsTimeField</code> answered for every registry at once, so a project resolving from both the public registry and a Verdaccio instance either paid for full metadata everywhere or claimed a <code>time</code> field npmjs does not serve. The answer is now per registry, and <code>registrySupportsTimeField</code> remains the answer for every registry that does not declare one.</p> <p>The declaration is also sent to a pnpr server, which applies it to the resolution it runs on the client's behalf.</p> </li> <li> <p>A pnpr resolve request now carries the client's registries the way the <code>registries</code> setting declares them — keyed by URL, with the scopes routed to each, the bare-specifier prefix each answers to, and each one's <code>serverType</code> — in place of the prefix map it used to send.</p> <p>The server routes them through the same inversion the config reader runs, so a pnpr-served install resolves a scoped dependency from the registry that scope is routed to, which it previously could not: only the default registry and the prefix-addressed ones reached the server. A declared <code>serverType</code> reaches it too, so the tarball URLs pnpr omits from the lockfile match the ones the client reconstructs.</p> <p>Built-in scope routes the project has not pointed elsewhere are not declared, so a pnpr server's allowlist is not asked about <code>npm.jsr.io</code> on requests that resolve no JSR package.</p> <p>A registry a request only declares is no longer refused up front for being off the server's allowlist — a client describes its whole configuration, including scopes a given resolve never reaches, so a stray <code>@scope:registry</code> in a developer's <code>~/.npmrc</code> no longer fails every install against a pnpr server that does not serve it. The boundary moves to the fetch itself: an origin the resolve does reach is refused before the request leaves the server, with the same message.</p> <p>This changes the resolve and verify-lockfile request bodies. A pnpr server and its clients have to be on matching versions; the protocol is still experimental and unversioned.</p> </li> <li> <p>A resolve request now carries the client's <code>resolutionMode</code>, so an install delegated to a pnpr server picks versions the way the client would. <code>time-based</code> and <code>lowest-direct</code> reached the server as nothing at all, leaving it on its <code>highest</code> default: the returned lockfile pinned the highest satisfying version of every dependency, and the setting appeared to be ignored.</p> <p>This adds a field to the resolve request body. A server older than its client ignores it and keeps resolving <code>highest</code>; the protocol is still experimental and unversioned.</p> </li> <li> <p>The <code>registries</code> setting now declares a registry once, keyed by its URL, with everything about that registry in the entry: how it lays out tarball URLs, the scopes routed to it, and the bare-specifier prefix it answers to.</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-yaml notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="registries: https://artifactory.example.com/artifactory/api/npm/npm-virtual/: serverType: artifactory scopes: ['@acme', '@acme-internal'] prefix: work"><pre><span class="pl-ent">registries</span>: <span class="pl-ent">https://artifactory.example.com/artifactory/api/npm/npm-virtual/</span>: <span class="pl-ent">serverType</span>: <span class="pl-s">artifactory</span> <span class="pl-ent">scopes</span>: <span class="pl-s">['@acme', '@acme-internal']</span> <span class="pl-ent">prefix</span>: <span class="pl-s">work</span></pre></div> <ul> <li><strong><code>serverType</code></strong> tells pnpm how the registry lays out its tarball URLs, which decides whether a URL can be omitted from <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code>: <ul> <li><strong>undeclared</strong> (the default) — strict. Only the exact canonical URL is treated as reconstructible.</li> <li><strong><code>npm</code></strong> — the registry behaves like <code>registry.npmjs.org</code>, which also serves a scoped package from its percent-encoded path. Declare this for a faithful mirror or caching proxy of the public registry so its tarball URLs can be omitted too.</li> <li><strong><code>artifactory</code></strong> — JFrog Artifactory repeats the scope in a scoped package's tarball filename (<code>@acme/widget/-/@acme/widget-1.0.0.tgz</code>) where the npm registry strips it (<code>@acme/widget/-/widget-1.0.0.tgz</code>). Declaring it lets pnpm rebuild that URL, so it is omitted from <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> instead of being written out for every scoped package <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/get-npm-tarball-url/issues/16" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/get-npm-tarball-url/issues/16/hovercard">pnpm/get-npm-tarball-url#16</a>.</li> </ul> </li> <li><strong><code>scopes</code></strong> lists the <code>@</code>-prefixed scopes that resolve from this registry. A bare <code>'@'</code> is the scope-less default registry, the one the <code>registry</code> setting names.</li> <li><strong><code>prefix</code></strong> is the alias a dependency addresses this registry by, as in <code>"foo": "work:^1.0.0"</code>.</li> </ul> <p>The layout is never inferred from the registry URL, so nothing changes unless you declare it; <code>registry.npmjs.org</code> continues to behave as <code>npm</code> without being declared. Because the lockfile depends on <code>serverType</code>, it is read from <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> only — a <code>serverType</code> in the global <code>config.yaml</code> is ignored, so one developer's machine cannot shape a lockfile their collaborators read back with a different layout. Credentials are rejected in this setting, in a key as well as in a field, and still belong in <code>.npmrc</code>. An entry that routes nothing to itself and matches no configured registry is reported as a warning rather than silently ignored.</p> <h3>Migrating</h3> <p>The older <code>registries</code> shape, a map of <code><scope>: <url></code> strings, still works and needs no change:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-yaml notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="registries: '@acme': https://npm.acme.example/"><pre><span class="pl-ent">registries</span>: <span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds">'</span><span class="pl-ent">@acme</span><span class="pl-pds">'</span></span>: <span class="pl-s">https://npm.acme.example/</span></pre></div> <p><code>namedRegistries</code> is deprecated in favor of the <code>prefix</code> field, and is still read for prefixes <code>registries</code> does not declare.</p> <p><code>toLockfileResolution</code> and <code>isCanonicalRegistryTarballUrl</code> now take their registry and layout as an options object rather than positional arguments, so <code>@pnpm/lockfile.utils</code> and <code>@pnpm/resolving.tarball-url</code> get a major bump.</p> </li> <li> <p>Added <code>virtualStoreType</code>, which names where the virtual store lives — one store per machine, or one per project:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-yaml notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="virtualStoreType: global # or: project"><pre><span class="pl-ent">virtualStoreType</span>: <span class="pl-s">global </span><span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">#</span> or: project</span></pre></div> <p>It is the canonical spelling of <code>enableGlobalVirtualStore</code>, which keeps working. When a project sets both, <code>virtualStoreType</code> wins. It can also be set through <code>PNPM_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_STORE_TYPE</code> and read back with <code>pnpm config get virtualStoreType</code>. The default is unchanged — <code>project</code>, so the shared store stays opt-in.</p> <p>The setting is independent of <code>nodeLinker</code>. <code>isolated</code> and <code>pnp</code> both work with either store type, and <code>hoisted</code> writes no virtual store at all, so it is unaffected.</p> </li> </ul> <h2>Patch Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm patch-commit</code> in project and edit paths containing non-ASCII characters.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>404</code> errors when installing from a registry that serves scoped packages only from a percent-encoded path, such as GitHub Enterprise Server. Outside <code>registry.npmjs.org</code>, a tarball URL that encodes the scope separator as <code>%2f</code> or <code>%2F</code> is no longer mistaken for one that pnpm can rebuild from the package name, version, and registry, so it is kept in <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> and requested verbatim on the next install <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13534" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13534/hovercard">#13534</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed an inconsistency where <code>minimumReleaseAgeExclude</code> (and <code>trustPolicyExclude</code>) wildcard/bare-name rules behaved differently in the evaluator and normalizer. A bare rule now consistently evaluates as matching every version, preventing unexpected behavior and silent widening of version policy exemptions when pnpm rewrites the workspace manifest <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13725" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13725/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13725</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm update --global --latest</code> failing with a 404 error when a globally installed package was not added from the registry by name. Packages installed from a local path (<code>link:</code>/<code>file:</code>), a git repository, a tarball URL, an <code>npm:</code> alias, or a named registry now keep their spec during a global update instead of being looked up by name in the default registry. See <a class="issue-link js-issue-link" data-error-text="Failed to load title" data-id="4838050440" data-permission-text="Title is private" data-url="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/12854" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/12854/hovercard" href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/12854">#12854</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm outdated</code> and <code>pnpm update --interactive</code> now dereference <code>catalog:</code> specifiers before querying the registry. A catalog entry that is an npm alias (<code>'@types/zkochan__table': npm:@types/table@6.3.2</code>) no longer fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_OUTDATED_REGISTRY_ERROR</code> for the alias key, and <code>pnpm outdated --compatible</code> compares against the range the catalog holds instead of skipping the dependency.</p> </li> <li> <p>A failed packument request now reports the status the registry returned (<code>404 Not Found</code>) instead of "error decoding response body".</p> </li> <li> <p>Installs with a cold cache are significantly faster: lockfile verification no longer delays resolution or downloads and re-checks far less data over the network, and downloaded packages are linked while the remaining downloads are still in flight.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm</code> installs using pnpr to honor the client's <code>autoInstallPeers</code>, <code>dedupePeers</code>, and <code>excludeLinksFromLockfile</code> settings <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13389" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13389/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13389</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>The three registry lookups are now named for what they are keyed by, so that none of them is called <code>registries</code> — a name the <code>registries</code> setting itself has taken:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>before</th> <th>after</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><code>Config.registries</code></td> <td><code>Config.registriesByScope</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>Config.namedRegistries</code></td> <td><code>Config.registriesByPrefix</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>Config.registryOptions</code></td> <td><code>Config.registryOptionsByUrl</code></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The same rename applies to the <code>RegistryContext</code> fields, the <code>Registries</code> and <code>NamedRegistries</code> types (now <code>RegistriesByScope</code> and <code>RegistriesByPrefix</code>), <code>normalizeRegistries</code> / <code>normalizeNamedRegistries</code> (now <code>normalizeRegistriesByScope</code> / <code>normalizeRegistriesByPrefix</code>), and the <code>BUILTIN_NAMED_REGISTRIES</code> constant (now <code>BUILTIN_REGISTRIES_BY_PREFIX</code>).</p> <p>This is an internal rename: no setting, error code, lockfile field, or <code>.pnpmfile.cjs</code> hook field changes. A <code>preResolution</code> hook still reads <code>ctx.registries</code>, which is the name pacquet passes as well. The <code>registries</code> and <code>namedRegistries</code> settings are read under the names users write them.</p> <p>The pnpr resolve request sends <code>registriesByPrefix</code> where it sent <code>namedRegistries</code>. A pnpr server and its clients must be on matching versions, which is already the case for an experimental server.</p> </li> <li> <p>An install that had to re-hash store files to verify them now reports it. If that cost more than a second, it says how long — <code>The integrity of N files was checked in 2.5s.</code> — and if it was quick but covered more than a thousand files, it names the cause instead: their timestamps changed since the store recorded them, which a backup tool, an antivirus scan or a copied store can do.</p> </li> <li> <p>Installs are faster in workspaces that declare inter-workspace dependencies with plain ranges (<code>"*"</code>, <code>"^1.2.3"</code>) rather than the <code>workspace:</code> protocol. With <code>preferWorkspacePackages</code> enabled, linking such a dependency no longer makes a registry request that cannot change the outcome — and workspace packages that were never published no longer cost a 404 on every install.</p> </li> <li> <p>An override change is now absorbed by the fast lockfile update even when another, unchanged override uses the <code>catalog:</code> protocol. Previously any <code>catalog:</code>-valued override forced a full re-resolution whenever the override list changed, which could move unrelated packages in the lockfile (for example after <code>pnpm audit --fix</code> added an override).</p> </li> <li> <p>Reduced peak memory usage when installing large packages. A tarball whose compressed size is at least 16 MiB, or whose registry-reported unpacked size is at least 64 MiB, is now extracted by streaming the decompression directly into the content-addressable store instead of materializing the whole decompressed archive in memory, and its large files are hashed and written to the store incrementally.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm why</code> and <code>pnpm list</code> no longer print stray <code>[90m</code>-style codes in their trees when the terminal supports colors. The bolded labels — the searched package in <code>pnpm why</code>, the project header and the matched package in <code>pnpm list</code> — dropped the escape byte of the styles they already carried, leaving the color codes as visible text.</p> </li> </ul>

## [NVIDIA Releases TensorRT Model Connect in Public Preview: Hugging Face Checkpoint to Native C++ Inference in Two Commands](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/08/18/nvidia-releases-tensorrt-model-connect-in-public-preview-hugging-face-checkpoint-to-native-c-inference-in-two-commands/)
*MarkTechPost* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: product_launch, open_source

> NVIDIA has released TensorRT Model Connect (TRTMC) in public preview, an Apache-2.0 project that takes a supported Hugging Face or local checkpoint to end-to-end TensorRT inference in two commands, with no intermediate ONNX export. The build emits a versioned .bundle artifact that runs through native C++ task APIs, so inference executes without PyTorch in the runtime path. NVIDIA's July 29, 2026 GB300 snapshot covers 105 release profiles across 76 model families. The post NVIDIA Releases TensorRT Model Connect in Public Preview: Hugging Face Checkpoint to Native C++ Inference in Two Commands appeared first on MarkTechPost .

## [Mojo🔥 is now open source](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/18/mojo-is-now-open-source/)
*Simon Willison's Blog* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: open_source, tool_update

> <p><strong><a href="https://www.modular.com/blog/mojo-open-source">Mojo🔥 is now open source</a></strong></p> The Mojo programming language has been promising an open source release <a href="https://simonwillison.net/2023/May/4/mojo/">since May 2023</a>. Last week they <a href="https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here">shipped their 1.0</a> and today they have followed through on that original promise, releasing the compiler and toolchain under an Apache 2 license.</p> <p>When Mojo first launched the stated goal was to produce a superset of Python, so existing Python code could be used to bootstrap their own ecosystem. That plan changed <a href="https://forum.modular.com/t/mojo-vision-document-and-roadmap/2187">around August 2025</a>:</p> <blockquote> <p>Mojo may or may not evolve into a full superset of Python, and it’s okay if it doesn’t.</p> <p>We’re encouraged by how well AI-assisted coding tools already help migrate Python to Mojo today, and we’re confident that future tooling and ecosystem maturity will make this evolution even smoother.</p> </blockquote> <p>Today Mojo is its own language, optimized to make GPU programming as painless as possible using syntax inspired by Python, if not 100% compatible with existing code. <p><small></small>Via <a href="https://lobste.rs/s/01lxuf/mojo_is_now_open_source">Lobste.rs</a></small></p> <p>Tags: <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/open-source">open-source</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/python">python</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/mojo">mojo</a></p>

## [Cartesia Ships Sonic-3.6: A Streaming TTS Model That Now Leads Both Artificial Analysis Speech Arenas](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/08/18/cartesia-ships-sonic-3-6-a-streaming-tts-model-that-now-leads-both-artificial-analysis-speech-arenas/)
*MarkTechPost* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: api_update, tool_update

> Cartesia has released Sonic-3.6, a streaming text-to-speech model built on state space models rather than transformers. It now ranks #1 on both Artificial Analysis speech leaderboards — 1,283 Elo on Provider Voice and 1,123 on Controlled Voice, the board that clones every model onto the same eight reference voices to isolate the synthesis engine. Cartesia states sub-90ms time-to-first-audio. The model is available in beta on Cartesia's own API The post Cartesia Ships Sonic-3.6: A Streaming TTS Model That Now Leads Both Artificial Analysis Speech Arenas appeared first on MarkTechPost .

## [pnpr 0.1.0-alpha.7](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/pnpr%400.1.0-alpha.7)
*GitHub Releases · pnpm* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: developer_tool, cli_tool

> <h2>Minor Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p>Packument responses now carry a <code>Last-Modified</code> header derived from the document's <code>time.modified</code>, so a client's release-age check can learn the package-level last-publish bound from a cheap <code>HEAD</code> probe instead of downloading the metadata body.</p> </li> <li> <p>A pnpr resolve request now carries the client's registries the way the <code>registries</code> setting declares them — keyed by URL, with the scopes routed to each, the bare-specifier prefix each answers to, and each one's <code>serverType</code> — in place of the prefix map it used to send.</p> <p>The server routes them through the same inversion the config reader runs, so a pnpr-served install resolves a scoped dependency from the registry that scope is routed to, which it previously could not: only the default registry and the prefix-addressed ones reached the server. A declared <code>serverType</code> reaches it too, so the tarball URLs pnpr omits from the lockfile match the ones the client reconstructs.</p> <p>Built-in scope routes the project has not pointed elsewhere are not declared, so a pnpr server's allowlist is not asked about <code>npm.jsr.io</code> on requests that resolve no JSR package.</p> <p>A registry a request only declares is no longer refused up front for being off the server's allowlist — a client describes its whole configuration, including scopes a given resolve never reaches, so a stray <code>@scope:registry</code> in a developer's <code>~/.npmrc</code> no longer fails every install against a pnpr server that does not serve it. The boundary moves to the fetch itself: an origin the resolve does reach is refused before the request leaves the server, with the same message.</p> <p>This changes the resolve and verify-lockfile request bodies. A pnpr server and its clients have to be on matching versions; the protocol is still experimental and unversioned.</p> </li> <li> <p>A resolve request now carries the client's <code>resolutionMode</code>, so an install delegated to a pnpr server picks versions the way the client would. <code>time-based</code> and <code>lowest-direct</code> reached the server as nothing at all, leaving it on its <code>highest</code> default: the returned lockfile pinned the highest satisfying version of every dependency, and the setting appeared to be ignored.</p> <p>This adds a field to the resolve request body. A server older than its client ignores it and keeps resolving <code>highest</code>; the protocol is still experimental and unversioned.</p> </li> </ul> <h2>Patch Changes</h2> <ul> <li>Fixed <code>pnpm</code> installs using pnpr to honor the client's <code>autoInstallPeers</code>, <code>dedupePeers</code>, and <code>excludeLinksFromLockfile</code> settings <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13389" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13389/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13389</a>.</li> </ul>

*MarkTechPost* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: open_source, tool_update

> Nous Research has shipped Bot Mode for Hermes Agent, its MIT-licensed open source agent. Bot Mode replaces the single-agent session list with a roster of named bots. Each bot is a real Hermes profile, with its own chat, memory, skills, and pinned model. It is now bundled and default-on in Hermes Desktop. ## [v8.0.0-rc.3](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/releases/tag/v8.0.0-rc.3)
*GitHub Releases · Prisma 7* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 0.92
Tags: api_update, cli_tool

> <h1>v8.0.0-rc.3</h1> <p>A single-purpose release: <code>@prisma/orm-toolchain</code> moves its exact <code>@prisma/cli-engine</code> peer from 0.1.1 to 0.2.0, so the unified <code>prisma</code> CLI can ship a release in which every mounted product runs on the one engine version it installs. There are no ORM API changes in this release.</p> <h2>Breaking changes</h2> <ul> <li><strong>The exact <code>@prisma/cli-engine</code> peer moves to 0.2.0</strong> — engine 0.2.0 adds the credential-refresh exports and structured delegated output that <code>prisma@8.0.0-rc.4</code> was built against but the registry's engine 0.1.1 does not contain, which is why <code>npx prisma@next</code> currently fails on import. This release pairs with the <code>prisma</code> CLI release that depends on it (<code>8.0.0-rc.5</code>); upgrade both together. No code changes — an operational peer move only. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/30056" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/30056/hovercard">#30056</a>)</li> </ul>
